name: Caesarism
summary: Caesarism is rule by a single strong leader who rises in a crisis of parties and parliament, claims legitimacy from direct popular acclaim or plebiscite, and leans on the army and a strong executive. Its paradigm cases are Napoleon Bonaparte and Napoleon III, whose 'social Caesarism' paired authoritarian order with concessions to workers, and Weber's plebiscitary leadership democracy supplies its analytic core.
scope: The plebiscitary-strongman strand as shown by Napoleon III's Second Empire (1852-70), Romieu's 1850 warlord version, Weber's plebiscitary leadership democracy and modern 'Red Caesarism' advocates. Gramsci, Marx and Spengler are analysts of Caesarism rather than adherents and are used only to document its mechanisms. It has no economic programme, so most answers outside leadership, army, plebiscites and parliament are inferred and low confidence.

keyFigures.name: Napoleon III
keyFigures.role: Ruler of France whose plebiscites and authoritarian-then-liberal Empire are the model of social Caesarism.

keyFigures.name: Max Weber
keyFigures.role: Sociologist who argued mass democracy tends toward plebiscitary, Caesarist leadership.

keyFigures.name: Auguste Romieu
keyFigures.role: Author of L'ère des Césars (1850), which framed Caesarism as military rule.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Social Caesarism courted workers with reforms, but no source ties it to health care, so a Caesarist ruler could go either way.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Wage-setting was no doctrinal point; Napoleon III's social policy aimed at winning workers, not at any wage floor.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The Second Empire both opened markets and drove state-backed public works and banks, so Caesarism takes no fixed line on markets versus state.

public-ownership.rationale: Napoleon III's railways and ports were built by encouraging private investment banks, so adherents lean away from nationalisation, inferred.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; a populist ruler wants mass favour but also depends on propertied backing.

unions-good.rationale: Napoleon III legalised strikes and association in the 1860s to win workers, yet Caesarism distrusts bodies independent of the leader; split.

property-fundamental.rationale: Marx records the bourgeoisie rallying to Bonaparte to save property and order, so property is protected, but the ruler is not bound by it.

regulate-corporations.rationale: No doctrine on corporate regulation; the Second Empire fostered finance and industry while directing public works.

cut-welfare.rationale: Social Caesarism used welfare-like concessions for workers, but nothing commits it to expanding or cutting programs.

worker-ownership.rationale: Caesarism poses the leader as arbiter above classes rather than handing enterprises to workers; inferred.

surveillance-ok.rationale: The Second Empire policed dissent heavily (mass arrests, licensed press), so security surveillance fits its logic; inferred.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Entirely outside Caesarist concerns; no basis to infer a position.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Not addressed; the regime restricted speech for order, not for protecting minorities, so adherents are split.

strong-leader.rationale: Caesarism is rule by a strong personal leader acting above parties and parliament; Weber's plebiscitary leadership democracy makes the same case.

state-harmful.rationale: Caesarism builds on a powerful executive state and army; Marx describes Bonaparte's bureaucracy and army as his instruments.

limit-guns.rationale: Not addressed; a strongman regime would restrict arms to opponents but this is not a doctrine.

empower-police-military.rationale: Army backing is central to Caesarism (Romieu's warlord rule) and Bonaparte's regime rested on army and police.

decide-locally.rationale: Caesarism concentrates power in the leader and his officials; the Second Empire governed through appointed prefects.

rehabilitation.rationale: No doctrine on punishment; order-focused rulers tend to be harsh but the sources do not say.

traditional-family.rationale: Marx's quote of the order party ("the family") shows order rhetoric defended it; inferred, not a Caesarist doctrine.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Anachronistic for the 19th-century core; modern Caesarists are split.

abortion-legal.rationale: Anachronistic and not part of Caesarist doctrine.

more-religion-public.rationale: Napoleon III backed the Church through the Falloux Law, while Böhmer's original sense was state control of the Church; split.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Not addressed by Caesarism as a doctrine.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Caesarist rulers cultivate national grandeur and tradition as a basis of mass loyalty; inferred.

gradual-change.rationale: Caesarism arises from crisis and decisive intervention, yet claims to restore order; Gramsci says it can be revolution or restoration.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Not addressed in the core literature.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Caesarism stresses national glory and a sovereign leader; supranational authority conflicts with this, inferred.

free-trade.rationale: Napoleon III signed the Cobden-Chevalier free-trade treaty, but trade policy is not a Caesarist doctrine.

nation-first.rationale: Napoleon III's foreign policy pursued French prestige and territory (Savoy, Nice); inferred as national interest first.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Napoleon III intervened abroad for glory and alliances, not clearly for human rights.

open-borders.rationale: A nationalist, order-centred rule is unlikely to favour open borders; inferred.

limit-growth.rationale: The Second Empire prized growth, railways and rebuilding Paris; inferred opposition to limiting growth.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Anachronistic; an executive could favour decisive action but no source says so.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Second Empire promoted industrial modernisation but there is no doctrine of technological salvation.

revolution-justified.rationale: Caesarist seizures like 2 December 1851 are framed as defence against revolution, while Caesar-type rule claims a mandate of its own; split.

experts-over-public.rationale: Weber wants leaders and officials over unstable mass opinion yet grounds the leader on mass acclaim; adherents split.

central-planning.rationale: Second Empire relied on private banks and markets with state works, so full planning is not a Caesarist aim; inferred.

socialized-markets.rationale: Not Caesarist; arbiter-above-classes rule does not hand firms to workers or the public.

land-value-tax.rationale: Land taxation never figured in Caesarist writing; the Second Empire's fiscal policy gives no lead.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Inheritance taxation is absent from the Caesarist literature and Napoleon III's rule left no clear stance.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: The Second Empire cut tariffs in 1860, but Caesarists are not committed to either trade policy.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Napoleon III's state drove railways, ports and Haussmann's Paris and encouraged investment banks; inferred as typical Caesarist practice.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Marx says Bonaparte's regime was built on the small-holding peasantry as its base; inferred sympathy for widespread small ownership.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Contrary to any Caesarist programme; inferred.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: The Second Empire promoted banks and finance rather than abolishing central institutions; inferred.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Some Caesarisms (Italian fascism) went corporatist, but the core literature does not.

one-party-rule.rationale: Caesarist legitimacy rests on a personal leader acclaimed by the masses, not on a guiding party; Weber's leader uses a machine but is not ruled by it.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Napoleon III turned a plebiscite into a hereditary empire, but Weber-style Caesarism is elective; split.

democracy-best.rationale: Weber sees mass democracy as demagogic and Spengler as ending in Caesarism; adherents honour popular acclaim but not voter-driven government.

direct-votes.rationale: Plebiscites are Caesarism's characteristic instrument, though they confirm the leader rather than vote on detailed laws.

workers-councils.rationale: Caesarism replaces councils and parliaments alike with personal executive rule; inferred.

right-to-secede.rationale: A strong centralising leader treats national unity as paramount; inferred.

natural-rulers.rationale: Weber holds that great charismatic individuals must make the soulless machinery of politics answer to values, in contrast to politicians without calling.

political-violence-never.rationale: Caesarist rule often begins with a coup (December 1851) and rests on the army, so violence is accepted when serving order.

war-builds-character.rationale: Spengler's Caesarism has martial themes but adherents are not shown to hold this literally.

separate-church-state.rationale: Böhmer's use implied the state's mastery over the Church, but Napoleon III favoured the Church; split.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Caesarist legitimacy is personal and popular, not scriptural; inferred.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Caesarism relies on the state's own army and police; inferred.

military-superiority.rationale: Army support and national glory are central to Caesarist rule; Napoleon III fought Crimea and Italy.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Not a core Caesarist concern; Napoleon III's empire was civic.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Social Caesarism tried to reconcile workers with the regime and place the leader above class conflict; inferred opposition.

equal-outcomes.rationale: No Caesarist egalitarian programme beyond social concessions; inferred.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Indigenous land rights lie outside the 19th-century Caesarist frame, and a centralising leader gives no basis for inference.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Caesarist regimes expanded colonies (Second Empire) and are unlikely to accept reparations; inferred.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Caesarism offers no ethic of self-interest; it glorifies the leader and nation, but is not hostile to it either.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Order and obedience to the leader outweigh individual liberties in Caesarist practice (press and dissent restrictions); inferred.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Environmental philosophy is not part of Caesarist doctrine, so no view can be inferred.

limit-population.rationale: Population control is not discussed in Caesarist sources.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Second Empire celebrated industrial progress; inferred.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Modernisation was welcomed but disruption of institutions is the opposite of Caesarist order.

human-enhancement.rationale: Bodily enhancement is anachronistic for Caesarism and no source gives a stance.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Weber's concern is human leaders overcoming impersonal machinery; handing rule to algorithms is the opposite; inferred.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: A regime that licensed the press and policed dissent would resist uncontrollable communication; inferred.

restore-past-order.rationale: Caesarism claims to save order but also to consolidate a revolution; Gramsci says progressive or reactionary depending on case.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Weber's leader judged by responsibility for results rather than doctrine; Gramsci warns against formulas; inferred.

direct-action.rationale: Caesarist coups are direct action by the elite, but direct action by the masses is not endorsed.

means-match-ends.rationale: Caesarism uses elections and force flexibly in service of the leader; inferred.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Wholly alien to a modern state-builder ideology; inferred.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Weber stresses necessary specialisation and bureaucracy in modern states; inferred.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Social Caesarism wanted to rally workers to the regime against liberal bosses, not to adopt the exploitation thesis; inferred.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Marx's own analysis treats Bonapartism as the counter-revolutionary rival of class dictatorship; Caesarists reject it.

collective-farming.rationale: The Bonapartist base was the small-holding peasantry; inferred.

taxation-theft.rationale: Caesarist states financed big public works through the state; inferred.

harm-principle.rationale: The Second Empire required permission for newspapers and exiled opponents, rejecting limits of state power to harm prevention.

individual-rights-only.rationale: No stated view on group rights.

conscription.rationale: An army-backed national leader normally accepts conscription; inferred.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Weber and Caesarists value voice through plebiscitary leadership; inferred.

state-as-business.rationale: Weber stresses legitimacy and leadership rather than customer service; inferred.

positive-liberty.rationale: Weber values freedom as capacity for meaningful action, but no Caesarist view on material means.

media-academia-power.rationale: Napoleon III controlled press and universities, implying their power was recognised; Caesarists not committed.

organic-representation.rationale: Caesarism builds on direct leader-mass ties rather than intermediary bodies; inferred.

total-state.rationale: Caesarism concentrates power in a leader but the Second Empire did not direct every sphere; inferred.

national-rebirth.rationale: Caesarist leaders from Napoleon to Mussolini promise national revival in a time of crisis; inferred.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Second Empire gained Savoy and Nice and expanded colonial holdings; inferred as typical.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Weber says charismatic rule rests on personal devotion, but feudal oaths are not Caesarist.

bound-labor.rationale: Contrary to Caesarism's mass-popular base; inferred.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Epistemology of power and truth is not a Caesarist concern; Weber's value-freedom view leans the other way but adherents are not committed.

universal-morality.rationale: Caesarism makes no claim about universal moral truths; legitimacy is charismatic and popular rather than moral-rational.

single-common-good.rationale: The Caesarist leader claims to arbitrate above rival factions in the national interest; inferred.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Caesarism has no position on Zionism; any modern Caesarist stance would depend on the leader.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: No Caesarist source addresses diaspora return or citizenship by return.

revive-national-language.rationale: Language revival is not part of Caesarism, though a nationalist leader could adopt it.

school-vouchers.rationale: The Falloux Law widened Church schooling, but vouchers are not addressed.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Large public works under Napoleon III imply borrowing tolerance, but no doctrine.

economic-freedom.rationale: Second Empire mixed economic liberalisation with political repression, which denies the claim.

rule-by-example.rationale: Caesarism relies on force and acclaim rather than moral example; inferred.

national-self-determination.rationale: Napoleon III backed Italian unification and a union of Danubian principalities; inferred, though not doctrinal.

force-without-un.rationale: A leader chasing national glory acts independently; Second Empire intervened abroad on its own terms (anachronistic).

reason-over-faith.rationale: Weber stresses charisma and passion in politics as well as reasoned responsibility; split.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Welfare eligibility for immigrants is anachronistic for the Second Empire and absent from Caesarist theory.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Welfare conditionality is not part of Caesarist doctrine; Napoleon III's social measures were about organisation of workers, not workfare.

class-collaboration.rationale: Napoleon III's social Caesarism paired authoritarian rule with social measures to rally workers against liberal employers, rejecting class struggle.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Napoleon III pursued grandeur but not destruction of cultural institutions; inferred.

dominated-front.rationale: A common front of countries dominated by the West is not a Caesarist idea; Napoleon III worked within European alliances.

workers-nation.rationale: Social Caesarism appealed to workers within the nation but no stated view on internationalism.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Caesarist writing is silent on gender roles in public life.

ban-interest.rationale: The regime encouraged investment banks and the stock market; inferred.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Caesarists present the leader as arbiter above contending classes, though Marx saw the Bonapartist state as serving a ruling class; inferred.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Energy policy is anachronistic for 19th-century Caesarism and not covered in modern accounts.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Immigrant assimilation is not addressed; a nationalist leader might favour it but sources are silent.

elite-replacement.rationale: A conspiracy thesis is not part of Caesarism; inferred.

proportional-representation.rationale: Caesarism's disdain for parliament and party politics implies opposition; inferred.

national-mission.rationale: Napoleon III spoke for national greatness but a missionary doctrine is not recorded.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Caesarism does not theorise gender hierarchy either way.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Weber saw parties failing to attract independent minds and Gramsci links Caesarism to a crisis of authority when parties stop representing groups; the populist case is anti-notables.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: The regime relied on army and police as its base; accountability for them is unlikely; inferred.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Public works, rebuilding Paris and active foreign policy show Caesarism wants a far wider state.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Weber vociferously supported equal suffrage and the regime kept universal male suffrage; inferred.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Caesarism has no analysis of settler states, and Second Empire colonial expansion points to no clear verdict.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Conversion law is not addressed; Napoleon III supported the Church but did not restrict conversion in the sources.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Cattle slaughter is wholly outside the Caesarist tradition.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: The Falloux Law expanded Catholic role in education under Napoleon III; inferred disagreement.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Caesarism grounds legitimacy in plebiscitary acclaim (the 1851 and 1852 plebiscites, Weber's Caesarist election), though the consent is thin.

trade-surplus.rationale: No stated view on trade balance.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: The December 1851 coup and Napoleon III's wars show Caesarism initiates force for its aims.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Spengler sees struggle but adherents not shown to hold the thesis.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: The Second Empire suppressed opposition and exiled opponents after the coup; inferred acceptance.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Caesarist rulers hold arbitrary power themselves; inferred rejection.

separated-powers.rationale: Executive supremacy over a weakened legislature is the core; Marx calls it force without phrases over the force of phrases and the 1852 constitution cut the Assembly's role.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Social Caesarism courted workers but no priority for the poor is stated.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Social housing sales are an anachronistic British issue that Caesarism never addressed.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Napoleon III both legalised strikes in the 1860s and policed dissent; split.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Malthusian causes of poverty are not discussed in Caesarist sources.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Caesarist theory concerns the form of rule, not ethnic diversity and cohesion, so no stance is documented.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Weber wants charismatic leaders, which lottery excludes; inferred.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Caesarism arises from crisis and claims arbiter powers; Napoleon III's coup and arrests of tens of thousands were justified by order.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Napoleon III's social Caesarism courted urban workers, but food price-fixing is not documented as doctrine.

party-controls-media.rationale: The Second Empire required government permission for political newspapers and could suspend them; government control rather than party control.

party-commands-army.rationale: Under Caesarism the leader himself commands the army, not a party; inferred.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Naturalization periods are not addressed in the Caesarist literature.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Caesarism has no commitment to rank-and-file politician pay; inferred.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Weber says the party machine serves the leader; discipline is useful but not a Caesarist principle.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Caesarism centres national sovereignty in a leader; inferred.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The 1852 constitution gave Napoleon III broad power over war, treaties and legislation, and Romieu defined Caesarism as warlord rule.

clerical-rule.rationale: Böhmer coined Caesarism for the state's subordination of the Church, so clerics holding supreme authority is contrary.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Caesarism is nationalist and army-backed; inferred.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: The regime licensed press but moral censorship of art is not recorded in sources.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: The 1852 constitution let the head of state be re-elected indefinitely through ten-year terms.

recall-officials.rationale: Weber's leader is not recallable between plebiscites; inferred.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Napoleon III used alliances (Britain in Crimea) but no doctrine.

people-in-arms.rationale: Caesarist rule relies on a professional army as its base; Marx describes the army as the regime's instrument.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Bonapartism drew on the peasantry but no moral view of rural life is recorded.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Napoleon III backed Italian unification but not as a general doctrine.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: The regime policed professors yet no such claim is attributed.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Spengler ranks civilizations as phases of life, but Caesarism as a political doctrine takes no position on cultural equality.

death-penalty.rationale: Capital punishment is not addressed in Caesarist sources, though order-minded rulers often retained it.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Sex education is anachronistic and outside Caesarism.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Science curriculum disputes are not part of Caesarism.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Not addressed; Second Empire censorship targeted politics rather than morals in the sources I opened.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Citizenship rules are not addressed by Caesarist authors.

minority-language-support.rationale: Minority-language policy is not addressed; a centralising nationalist leader would probably not prioritise it.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Exemptions from general law for religious minorities are not addressed in Caesarist literature.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Order and conformity under a ruler who policed the press; inferred.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Third-world debt is anachronistic for Caesarism and no source gives a view.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Napoleon III replaced assemblies with a plebiscitary constitution; inferred preference for leader-written constitutions.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The authoritarian Empire (1852-60) restricted press and politics while pushing railways, banking and rebuilding Paris.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Duties of global aid are not part of Caesarist thought, which centres the nation and leader.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Nuclear weapons are anachronistic for the core, though a leader prizing national glory and army would likely favour independence; sources are silent.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Plebiscitary election of the leader is the Caesarist mechanism: Weber's Caesarist election of a charismatic leader and Napoleon III's plebiscites.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Caesarist leaders subordinate institutions to their authority; inferred.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Territorial concessions are not addressed; Napoleon III gained Savoy and Nice but no doctrine on keeping homeland territory is recorded.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Caesarism defends property for order yet rules above class interests; split.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Environmental regulation is not part of Caesarist doctrine.

collective-defense.rationale: Napoleon III formed alliances for specific wars but no doctrine.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Napoleon III annexed Savoy and Nice with a plebiscite; position on unconsented annexation not stated.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Böhmer's coinage meant state mastery of the Church but Napoleon III favoured the Church through the Falloux Law; split.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: The Caesarist leader stands above parties but as an active ruler through a machine, not a symbol; split.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: A centralising national leader would defend territorial unity by force; inferred.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Centralised rule leaves little room for regional systems; inferred.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Caesarist authority is charismatic and plebiscitary, not divine descent; inferred.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Tax structure is absent from Caesarist sources; the Second Empire gives no lead.

character-from-environment.rationale: Caesarism has no theory of human nature versus upbringing, though Weber's stress on charisma hints at innate gifts.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Caesarist rulers claim a popular mandate above ordinary legal constraints, as in the 1852 constitution; inferred.

space-expansion.rationale: Space policy is anachronistic and absent from Caesarism.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Weber pairs a plebiscitary leader with parliament as a check on him, though Caesarism proper reduces parliament; split.

leader-cult.rationale: Weber treats personal devotion to a leader as the basis of charismatic rule and Schwentzel notes public desire for authority and grandeur.

equal-parenting.rationale: Family-court presumptions are outside Caesarist concerns.

land-redistribution.rationale: Bonapartism rested on existing smallholding peasants and propertied order; inferred.

refugee-return.rationale: Refugee return is not addressed in Caesarist sources.

common-currency.rationale: Monetary union is not addressed; the Second Empire helped the Latin Monetary Union era but sources give no Caesarist doctrine.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Pan-ethnic unions are not addressed by Caesarist authors.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Minority cultural self-government is not addressed in Caesarist writing and sits awkwardly with a centralising leader.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Caesarism has no stance on persecuted minorities choosing between emigration and local rights struggle.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Caesarists, like Weber, stress leadership and values over economic determinism; inferred.

ban-cartels.rationale: Antitrust is not part of Caesarism; the Second Empire promoted large investment banks without a stated view on concentration.

no-bailouts.rationale: Bailouts are an anachronistic question; Caesarist rulers tend to be pragmatic about them, but sources give no view.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Plebiscitary leadership democracy puts the leader acclaimed by the majority above institutional limits; inferred.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: The Second Empire opened trade by treaty; inferred.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Modern trade-agreement standards are anachronistic and not addressed by Caesarism.

moral-incentives.rationale: Moral incentives are a socialist theme not found in Caesarist literature.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Caesarist coups are by the army or leader, not guerrilla revolution; split.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Caesarism is anti-notable populism, but Napoleon III built a new court nobility; split.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Curriculum framing is not addressed, though a nationalist leader plausibly favours national history.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Second Empire expanded colonial holdings substantially; inferred.

patriotic-education.rationale: The education minister controlled professors and curricula under Napoleon III; inferred approval of loyalty teaching.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: US-style racial preference debates are outside Caesarism.

public-money-creation.rationale: Monetary reform ideas are not part of Caesarist doctrine.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Caesarism is neither Marxist nor liberal-economic here; the Second Empire's investment boom suggests optimism, but adherents give no view.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Napoleon III's Mexico intervention was an influence project but no doctrine.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: A Leninist theory about workers in rich countries is not addressed in Caesarist literature.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Private discrimination rights are not addressed in Caesarist sources.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Caesarists place the leader above entrenched limits; inferred.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Caesarist authors do not address colonial-era treaties.

elective-rulers.rationale: The Caesarist ruler is chosen by popular plebiscite or acclaim rather than hereditary right, though Napoleon III later made the empire hereditary.

minority-veto.rationale: Plebiscitary rule enforces the mass will against dissent; inferred.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Caesarism's ruler legitimates himself by plebiscite, not constitutional trust; inferred.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Weber shows disdain for parliament and Marx describes executive victory over the legislature as force without phrases.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Animal ethics is not part of Caesarist doctrine.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Animal use regulations are not addressed in Caesarist sources.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Caesarism courts the masses against notables rather than preaching aristocratic duty, but social Caesarism had paternal elements; no clear view.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Caesarism depends on mass political engagement through acclaim; inferred.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Critical theory of mass culture is not Caesarist, though Weber's demagogy concern is related; no clear view.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Gramsci analyses hegemony but adherents are not shown to hold this view.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Dependency theory is not part of Caesarist thought.

native-born-offices.rationale: Office eligibility by birth is not addressed in Caesarist literature.

party-own-road.rationale: Debate on communist party autonomy is outside Caesarism.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Development strategy is not addressed in Caesarist writing.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Napoleon III's wars gained territory but no stated revanchist doctrine.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Mussolini embraced Caesarism, but modern Caesarists are split on this.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Mussolini embraced Caesarism, so modern Caesarists are split on equating fascism with communism; no firm view.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: American historiography is not part of Caesarist doctrine.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Monument policy is not addressed, though a leader-cult tradition favours public commemoration; no firm view.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Gendered social programmes are not addressed by Caesarism.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Domestic violence policy is not addressed by Caesarism.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Caesarism claims a universal pattern (Weber, Spengler) emerging from democracy rather than civilization-specific institutions; no firm view.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Romieu defined Caesarism as military rule and Gramsci treats generals claiming to defend the national good as Caesarism's typical agents.

paid-care-work.rationale: Unpaid care work is not addressed in Caesarist sources.

filial-duty.rationale: Family duty is not addressed in the sources, though order rhetoric usually supports it.

office-by-exam.rationale: Napoleon III's state used appointed officials, but examination-based recruitment is not a Caesarist principle.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Foreign ownership restrictions conflict with Second Empire openness to investment but are not addressed as doctrine.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Divorce law is not addressed in Caesarist sources.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Weber's leader answers to the plebiscite, not to binding instructions; inferred.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Pension design is anachronistic and absent from Caesarist writing.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Communal land tenure is not part of Caesarism; Bonapartism's base was peasant smallholders, but no view is documented.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: The 1852 constitution reduced the National Assembly's authority and gave the executive broad power.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Caesarism is a form of rule and says nothing on whether political independence requires economic transformation.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Napoleon III backed nationalities in Italy and Romania, but a general claim to territory for co-nationals abroad is not a Caesarist principle.

delink-world-market.rationale: Napoleon III signed free-trade treaties and promoted investment; delinking is not a Caesarist idea, so inferred disagreement.

missingStatements.text: A national leader should be confirmed in power by direct popular plebiscites rather than only by parliament.
missingStatements.rationale: Plebiscitary legitimation is the defining Caesarist mechanism, from Napoleon III's 1851-52 votes to Weber's Caesarist election of a leader.

notes: Caesarism is a mechanism of rule rather than a programme, so adherents ranged from progressive (Gramsci's Caesar, Napoleon III's social policy) to reactionary (Mussolini, Red Caesarism). Almost every economic and cultural answer is inferred.
